```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(knitr)
library(tidyverse)

# blue-ish palette for the matrix heatmaps
mat_cols <- colorRampPalette(c("white", "steelblue", "#3C5454"))(50)
```



## Many variables in many samples

As in all _omic_ experiments, a metabolomic assay measures a large number of **variables** (properties) in a (hopefully) reasonably large number of **samples**.

<div class="box-red">
⚠️ <strong>Question:</strong> <br> ... what are the variables ...
</div>

::: incremental
1. In a targeted metabolomics investigation?
2. In an untargeted MS based metabolomics analysis?
3. In an untargeted NMR based metabolomics assay?
:::


## Number of variables | place your guess

::: fragment
* Targeted metabolomics investigation
    * ~~from 10 to 300~~
:::

::: fragment
* Untargeted metabolomics investigation
    * ~~from 1000 to 30000~~
:::


## Data Matrix

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width="60%"}
include_graphics("../images/Matrix.svg")
```


## The goal of data analysis

<div class="box-red">
⚠️ <strong>Goal:</strong> <br> The objective of data analysis is to find **"organization"** inside the matrix
</div>

::: {.box-key .fragment}
Our organization should also be statistically robust: if someone redid my experiment, the results should be the same 😉
:::


## Organization: Correlations

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=6, fig.height=5, out.width="55%"}
set.seed(42)
n <- 150
rho_target <- 0.8

# Y = rho * X + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * noise  ->  cor(X, Y) ~ rho
X <- rnorm(n)
Y <- rho_target * X + sqrt(1 - rho_target^2) * rnorm(n)

tibble(X = X, Y = Y) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = X, y = Y)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7, size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "#8B3A3A", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Variable X", y = "Variable Y") +
  theme_light(base_size = 16)
```


## Organization: Biomarkers

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=6, fig.height=5, out.width="55%"}
set.seed(123)
n <- 50

data_sig <- tibble(
  Group = rep(c("Control", "Treatment"), each = n),
  Variable_A = c(rnorm(n, mean = 10, sd = 2), rnorm(n, mean = 13, sd = 2))
)

ggplot(data_sig, aes(x = Group, y = Variable_A, fill = Group)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.3, alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Control = "steelblue", Treatment = "orange")) +
  labs(x = "Group", y = "Variable A") +
  theme_light(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```


# Data Matrices: facts

## Variables are not independent

<div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 30px;">
<div style="flex: 1;">

::: incremental
* Biological relations
* Chemical/Analytical reasons
:::

</div>
<div style="flex: 1;">
```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5, out.width="90%"}
set.seed(1)
tibble(Var1 = 1:20, Var2 = Var1 * 2 + rnorm(20, 0, 3)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Var1, y = Var2)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#8B3A3A", size = 3) +
  ggtitle("Correlation") +
  theme_light(base_size = 16) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```
</div>
</div>


## Analytical vs biological correlation

<div class="box-red">
⚠️ <strong>Important:</strong> <br> Analytical correlation is always stronger than the biological one!
</div>

::: {.box-key .fragment}
The correlation structure of your matrix is often not really informative about biology
:::


## Rows (samples) are often dependent

The design of the study can result in a ~~multilevel hierarchical structure~~ of the samples which violates independence. In other words some samples are "by construction" associated and share something in common

**Examples**

::: incremental
1. Repeated measures of the same individual
2. Subpopulations
3. Different sites, different days, ...
:::


## Data Matrix size

In the typical "happy" statistical context, the number of variables we measure is smaller than the number of samples.

In _omics_ the number of variables normally exceeds the number of samples

```{r fig.align='center', fig.height=1.6, fig.width=12, out.width="100%"}
set.seed(2)
mymat <- matrix(rnorm(20 * 300), nrow = 20)
par(mar = c(2, 2, 0, 0))
image(t(mymat), col = mat_cols, asp = 20/300, xlab = "", ylab = "", axes = FALSE)
mtext("Variables", side = 1, line = 0.5)
mtext("Samples", side = 2, line = 0.5)
```

::: {.box-key .fragment}
FAT DATA MATRIX
:::


# Analyzing data matrices

## Univariate approach

The **Univariate** approach considers each variable separately and applies "standard" statistical tools to spot the more **interesting** variables

::: incremental
1. Statistical testing
2. Linear modeling (`lm`, `glm`, ...)
3. ANOVAs
4. Hierarchical Modeling
:::

```{r fig.align='center', fig.height=2.5, fig.width=6, out.width="60%"}
set.seed(3)
mymat <- matrix(rnorm(20 * 100), nrow = 20)
par(mar = rep(0, 4), xpd = NA)
image(t(mymat), col = mat_cols, asp = 20/100, xaxt = "n", ann = FALSE, yaxt = "n", bty = "n")
for (x in c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)) {
  rect(xleft = x, xright = x + 0.01, ybottom = -0.1, ytop = 1.1, border = "#8B3A3A", lwd = 3)
}
```


## Univariate: pros and cons

::::: cols
::: {.col .box-lightgreen}
**PRO** 😀

1. Statistical modeling is there!
2. Interpretable by construction
:::

::: {.col .box-red .fragment}
**CONS** 😞

1. Multiple testing
2. The structure of the data creates redundancy
3. Assumptions for parametric (and non parametric) approaches are often not fulfilled
:::
:::::


## Where is the problem: Multiple testing

::: incremental
* We measure many variables (features, metabolites) in the same set of samples
* We run a battery of statistical tests looking for the significance of what we see in the individual variables
* **We ask ourselves if at least one test is significant in the overall set of tests**
:::

::: {.box-key .fragment}
We run individual tests, but we have a question about the full set of variables ...
:::


## Multivariate approach

Each sample is represented as a point in the multidimensional variable space. The dataset is a **cloud** of points in that space.

The size of the space equals the number of variables we are measuring. **Multivariate methods** (PCA, PLS, ASCA, ...) are able to exploit the correlation between the variables to highlight/extract the organization of the data

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width="35%"}
include_graphics("../images/Coord_planes_color.svg")
```


## Why multivariate ...

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5, out.width="40%"}
# points on an ellipse with given center, semi-axes and rotation
generate_ellipse <- function(center = c(0, 0), axes = c(1, 0.5), angle = 0, n_points = 100) {
  theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n_points)
  xy <- rbind(axes[1] * cos(theta), axes[2] * sin(theta))
  rot <- matrix(c(cos(angle), -sin(angle), sin(angle), cos(angle)), nrow = 2)
  rotated <- t(rot %*% xy)
  tibble(x = rotated[, 1] + center[1], y = rotated[, 2] + center[2])
}

ellipses <- bind_rows(
  generate_ellipse(center = c(-1.5, 0), axes = c(2, 1), angle = pi / 6) |> mutate(group = "A"),
  generate_ellipse(center = c(1.5, 1), axes = c(2, 1), angle = pi / 6) |> mutate(group = "B")
)

ggplot(ellipses, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = group, colour = group)) +
  geom_polygon(alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-1.5, 1.5), y = c(0, 1), label = c("A", "B"), size = 7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(A = "steelblue", B = "orange")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(A = "steelblue", B = "orange")) +
  labs(x = "Var 1", y = "Var 2") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_light(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.box-key .fragment}
Group separation is clearer in the 2D space ...
:::


## Multivariate: pros and cons

::::: cols
::: {.col .box-lightgreen}
**PRO** 😀

1. Potentially more powerful
2. Explicit use of variable correlation
3. No issues with multiple testing
:::

::: {.col .box-red .fragment}
**CONS** 😞

1. Chance correlations in fat matrices
2. Empty space
3. Difficult to embed hierarchical structure
:::
:::::


## The problem: the curse of dimensionality

```{r fig.align='center', fig.height=2.5, fig.width=8, out.width="100%"}
set.seed(123)
pt_col <- adjustcolor("orange", alpha.f = 0.6)

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), pty = "s")
plot(y = rep(0, 10), x = runif(10, 0, 10), xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n", bty = "n", xlim = c(-1, 11),
     main = "10 points 1D", xlab = "", ylab = "", col = pt_col, cex = 2, pch = 19)
arrows(x0 = 0, y0 = 0, x1 = 11)
plot(y = runif(10, 0, 10), x = runif(10, 0, 10), xlab = "D1", ylab = "D2",
     main = "10 points 2D", col = pt_col, cex = 2, pch = 19)
plot(y = runif(100, 0, 10), x = runif(100, 0, 10), xlab = "D1", ylab = "D2",
     main = "100 points 2D", col = pt_col, cex = 2, pch = 19)
```

::: incremental
1. To fill the space, the number of points does not grow linearly with the number of dimensions
2. Already with 10 samples the 2D plot looks empty
:::

::: {.box-key .fragment}
Can you imagine 20 samples in 10000 dimensions? 😉
:::
